full_text: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has declared its seventeenth Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which had been circulating undetected for months. The response is now catching up across a region weakened by conflict, displacement and loss of humanitarian aid. With no licensed vaccine or treatment, containment will depend on rebuilding resources, access and trust in public health systems. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and its neighbouring countries face an incredible challenge in the new Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) disease outbreak. By the time the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in Kinshasa confirmed BDBV in Ituri Province, officials had already recorded 246 suspected cases and 80 suspected deaths across several health zones. Confirmed cases were soon logged across multiple DRC provinces and in Kampala, the capital of neighbouring Uganda1. The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 17 May, and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention followed with a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security on 18 May, naming ten other countries at high risk of spread2,3. The scale of those initial figures made it evident that the world was not discovering a new outbreak so much as uncovering one that had been silently circulating, hidden by the fragility of local healthcare capacity and propagated by conflict, community distrust and population mobility. As of 31 May, 336 cases had been confirmed across both countries, with 49 confirmed deaths, alongside 220 suspected cases and 236 suspected deaths in the DRC. These numbers are almost certainly an undercount. A modelling group at Imperial College London estimated within days of the declaration that true infections probably already exceeded 900, and many community deaths have never entered a formal record4. Unlike West Africa in 2013, where the index case seeded a region with no prior filovirus experience, the DRC and its neighbours have extensive experience with viral haemorrhagic fevers, including 10 outbreaks in the past 5 years alone. The communities and health workers of the region have shown remarkable resilience across these repeated emergencies, carrying the burden of response, often at great personal cost, with limited and intermittent external support. However, a confluence of factors is lining up to make this outbreak at least the second-biggest Ebola crisis the world has seen. First, delayed laboratory identification allowed geographic expansion, and the response is now playing catch-up. The initial delay followed negative Ebola testing at the provincial laboratory in Bunia, which required specimens to be sent to Kinshasa for species-specific confirmation. Even before the 5 May alert to the WHO, some unexplained illnesses had been noted in the region with negative testing for common pathogens, highlighting regional blind spots leading to the current crisis, which may have resulted from sudden withdrawal of aid. The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) was historically the DRC’s largest humanitarian donor and since its dissolution the DRC has seen surge in cholera, mpox and measles across its eastern provinces, conditions under which an uncommon disease is far harder to distinguish from the common ones5. Although most cases remain in Ituri, patients have been confirmed hundreds of kilometres away in North and South Kivu Provinces, in eastern DRC. These multiple fronts require already-strained resources — treatment units, infection prevention and sanitation supplies, contact tracers, laboratory capacity and community engagement — to be divided even further. Financial commitments have been made by the national government and the global community, but there is typically a lag between the appropriation of funds and their conversion into contracts, procurement and distribution, making this the most precarious moment of the response. Reports from affected areas indicate that personal protective equipment and diagnostic supplies are severely lagging behind need6. Active conflict is impeding access, and that conflict has worsened with the withdrawal of aid that followed the dismantling of USAID. On 28 May, the WHO Director-General travelled to the DRC to appeal for a ceasefire, enabling central outbreak control efforts to continue: bringing sick patients into isolation, assuring them they will be safe as they receive care, and tracing their contacts across an insecure terrain. In this outbreak, trust is as valuable and critical as monetary funds. A population-based survey during the 2018–2019 North Kivu outbreak found that only about a third of respondents trusted that local authorities represented their interests, and a quarter believed the outbreak was not real7. During that outbreak, the WHO recorded roughly 390 attacks on health facilities and workers in 2019 (ref. 8). The same dynamics are now compounded by displacement and the loss of the previously funded community programmes. Because there have been only two previous outbreaks, research on BDBV medical countermeasures lags between that for Zaire and Sudan ebolaviruses, for which there are either approved products or more products with safety and efficacy data. Although arrangements for vaccine and therapeutic trials are underway, the manufacturing and trial timelines mean deployment is likely to be months away9. Their capacity to alter the trajectory of this outbreak, at least in the near term, is therefore limited. And that trajectory is concerning. The outbreak will probably continue for months, potentially into 2027, with a high risk of spread into areas hosting displaced and refugee populations and across borders, making regional collaboration essential. Although BDBV is unlikely to cause a pandemic, as cases rise, sporadic suspect cases may surface in travellers worldwide, particularly given the nonspecific early symptoms of Ebola. Despite the alarm these cases generate, the base rate of true infection among travellers is very low, and the overwhelming majority of suspected cases evaluated elsewhere will test negative. BDBV mortality has ranged from 30% to 50% in the historical record, lower than the roughly 40–66% seen in large Zaire ebolavirus outbreaks. But those estimates rest on a small number of patients, and case fatality rates shift over the arc of an outbreak. Early mortality may be high, reflecting delays in reaching care and a shortage of treatment resources. As more resources arrive, a falling case fatality rate would indicate two improvements at once: better success in building trust and bringing patients in, and better supportive care once they arrive. The current numbers could be read as a measure of the response’s reach as well as the virus’s lethality. Lastly, the current outbreak is occurring in the middle of another underlying shift: US global aid architecture is shifting towards new approaches, such as ‘America First’ bilateral agreements, rather than investment in multilateral and sector-wide health programmes. African countries are re-examining how regional commitments can be consolidated to build a safer, more self-reliant future10. The containment of Bundibugyo virus outbreak, and the inevitable outbreaks that will follow it, will require consistent commitment on both fronts at once: regional investment that builds standing capacity where these viruses emerge, and global solidarity that is durable rather than episodic. A reactive posture, in which funding is surged only after a crisis has occurred, leaves us backfooted, particularly in areas of complex humanitarian emergencies. This creates massive gaps in timely resources, the cost of which is paid in patient lives and healthcare worker safety. References - World Health Organization. source_body_en: The Democratic Republic of the Congo has declared its seventeenth Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which had been circulating undetected for months. The response is now catching up across a region weakened by conflict, displacement and loss of humanitarian aid. With no licensed vaccine or treatment, containment will depend on rebuilding resources, access and trust in public health systems. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and its neighbouring countries face an incredible challenge in the new Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) disease outbreak. By the time the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in Kinshasa confirmed BDBV in Ituri Province, officials had already recorded 246 suspected cases and 80 suspected deaths across several health zones. Confirmed cases were soon logged across multiple DRC provinces and in Kampala, the capital of neighbouring Uganda1. The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 17 May, and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention followed with a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security on 18 May, naming ten other countries at high risk of spread2,3. The scale of those initial figures made it evident that the world was not discovering a new outbreak so much as uncovering one that had been silently circulating, hidden by the fragility of local healthcare capacity and propagated by conflict, community distrust and population mobility. As of 31 May, 336 cases had been confirmed across both countries, with 49 confirmed deaths, alongside 220 suspected cases and 236 suspected deaths in the DRC.
